list.listitem: Patient history and physical exam guide the rational use of sequential laboratory and imaging studies for diagnosing monoarticular arthritis. Patients with a history of trauma or focal bone pain require radiographs of the affected joint to rule out fracture, tumor, or metabolic bone disease. C

If a joint effusion is present in the absence of trauma, particularly if other signs of inflammation are also present, infection must be considered first. If reasonable concern for infection exists, arthrocentesis is mandatory. C

Synovial fluid WBC count below the inflammatory range (>2000 cells/mm3) can entirely exclude infection, although the likelihood of infection increases significantly as the synovial fluid WBC count rises to higher levels, particularly above 25,000 cells/mm3. B
Noninflammatory synovial fluid (<2000 cells/mm3) suggests osteoarthritis (OA) or internal derangement of the joint. Hemarthrosis suggests coagulopathy, trauma, tumor, pseudogout, or Charcot joint. C

Inflammatory synovial fluid containing monosodium urate crystals generally establishes the diagnosis of gout . Presence of podagra, particularly in the setting of hyperuricemia, indicates a high probability for the diagnosis of gout . Absence of detected crystals, particularly for pseudogout, does not exclude crystal-induced arthritis. B

background.definition: Monoarticular arthritis refers to the clinical presentation of pain or swelling in a single joint. Any condition that can cause joint pathology can initially present as monoarticular arthritis, resulting in an extremely broad differential diagnosis. Three primary diagnostic categories that cause monoarticular pain and swelling must be considered urgently: infection, trauma, and crystal-induced arthritis (gout and pseudogout).

list.listitem: Estimated annual incidence of septic arthritis is 2-6 per 100,000 population. Among patients with a prosthetic joint, an incidence rate of 1.5 infections per 1000 person–joint-years was found for hip or knee arthroplasty in a population-based study; most occurred in the first year following surgery.
In a 10-year case series of 892 patients presenting to an urban hospital with a swollen, painful wrist without trauma and underwent joint fluid analysis, 1.5% had septic arthritis.

In 2015-16, the overall prevalence of gout among US adults was 3.9%, with a total affected population of 9.2 million. An earlier study revealed a higher prevalence in men than women (5.9% and 2.0%, respectively).

Authors of a systematic review identified 4 studies including 363 patients reporting on prevalence of conditions responsible for monoarticular arthritis. The major causes were gout (15%–27%), septic arthritis (8%–27%), osteoarthritis (5%–17%), and rheumatoid arthritis (11%–16%), although the cause remained unknown in 16% to 36% of patients.
Avascular necrosis of bone: Associated with corticosteroid use and rheumatic diseases.

Bacterial infections, nongonococcal: The most common etiologic agents reported in large series of septic arthritis cases were (1) staphylococci, 44% to 70%, (2) streptococci, 15% to 35%, and (3) gram-negative organisms, 10% to 21%. Methicillin-resistant staph has been identified in 10% to 50% of cases with septic arthritis of native joints, primarily in patients with chronic illness, older age, or health care exposure. Although the vast majority of cases of septic arthritis (>90%) present as monoarticular arthritis, polyarticular cases can be seen through hematogenous spread in addition to other causes.

Crystal-induced arthritis: Presents as gout from monosodium urate crystals, pseudogout from calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals, or other crystal-induced arthritis from calcium oxalate or hydroxyapatite crystals. Septic arthritis can occur concomitantly in patients with crystal-induced arthritis. In one case series, 5% of joints with crystal arthritis had concomitant infection.

Drugs: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are associated with rheumatic symptoms mimicking rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, and other conditions. Although any joint can be affected, joints most commonly involved are the shoulders, MCP and PIP joints of the hands (around 50%), followed by knees and wrists (40%).
Gonococcal monoarticular arthritis: Results from hematogenous seeding of the joint from mucosal sites of primary gonococcal infection.

Hemarthrosis: May result from trauma, intra-articular fracture, excessive anticoagulation, inherited coagulopathies, pseudogout, Charcot joint, synovial hemangiomas, or pigmented villonodular synovitis.

Lyme arthritis: Usually presents as monoarthritis as a late manifestation of Lyme disease occurring in a large joint, often intermittently. In a French study of 37 patients with a positive PCR on synovial fluid for Borrelia, monoarticular was present in 92% and the knee was involved in 97%.
Mycobacterial and fungal arthritis: Presents typically in an immunocompromised patient.
Neuropathic joint (Charcot joint): Often presents secondary to diabetic neuropathy and is also seen in syphilis.
Osteoarthritis: May present as a flare of pain and swelling in a single joint associated with overuse or minor trauma.

Systemic diseases that cause oligo and polyarticular forms of arthritis can also present as monoarthritis: Spondyloarthropathies including psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, ankylosing spondyloarthritis, and also sarcoidosis or Behcet's disease. Less commonly, rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus, and forms of vasculitis present with monoarthritis.
Trauma: Presents with peri- and intra-articular factures, internal derangement of intra-articular structures, penetrating injuries commonly including thorns and wood fragments.
Tumors (peri-articular and intra-articular): include pigmented villonodular synovitis, chondrosarcoma, osteogenic sacoma, metastatic tumors, or osteoid osteoma.

Miscellaneous and less common causes: Amyloidosis, lipoma arborescens, synovial osteochondromatosis, viral-associated arthritis (eg, parvo virus, hepatitis B), relapsing polychondritis, and familial Mediterranean fever.
Pathophysiology depends on the specific cause of the monoarticular arthritis.
Patients with a history of trauma or focal bone pain require radiographs of the affected joint to rule out fracture, tumor, or metabolic bone disease. C

If joint effusion is present in the absence of trauma, and particularly if other signs of inflammation are also present, infection must be considered. If there is reasonable concern for infection, arthrocentesis is mandatory. C

Higher synovial fluid WBC counts increase the likelihood of infection, particularly above 25,000 cells/mm3, but no synovial fluid WBC cutoff within the inflammatory range (>2000 cell/mm3) can exclude infection. B

Noninflammatory synovial fluid (<2000 cells/mm3) suggests the possibility of OA or internal derangement of the joint. Hemarthrosis suggests the possibility of a coagulopathy, trauma, tumor, pseudogout, or Charcot joint. C

Inflammatory fluid containing monosodium urate crystals generally establishes the diagnosis of gout. There is less certainty in identifying crystals for pseudogout. The presence of podagra, particularly in the setting of hyperuricemia, provides a high probability for the diagnosis of gout. The absence of detected crystals, particularly for pseudogout, does not exclude crystal-induced arthritis. B
Patient history and physical exam often provide essential information to eliminate or focus on specific conditions in the differential diagnosis of monoarticular arthritis.
History of trauma? If so, obtain radiographs to rule out fracture or dislocation.

Do symptoms suggest a mechanical process or an inflammatory process? Mechanical joint pain typically worsens with activity and improves with rest. Inflammatory arthritis stiffens with rest, especially overnight, producing morning stiffness.

Is condition truly monoarticular? Any prodromal arthralgia symptoms suggesting systemic illness, particularly infections? Gonococcal arthritis is often preceded or accompanied by migratory arthritis and tenosynovitis before it settles in a primary joint as a purulent arthritis. Are there symptoms consistent with axial skeleton inflammatory arthritis, such as sacroiliitis, in addition to symptoms in a single peripheral joint that suggest a spondyloarthropathy?

Is condition acute? Hyperacute onset of joint pain and swelling suggests internal derangement, fracture, or trauma. Acute onset over hours or a couple days is typical of acute inflammatory conditions, including septic arthritis and crystal-induced arthritis, although occasionally inflammatory arthritis associated with systemic disease such as spondyloarthropathies or RA can present with surprisingly rapid onset.

Is the condition chronic or an exacerbation of a prior condition? For example, recurrent gout flare or an exacerbation of OA? It is important, however, to consider a superimposed disease in a patient with preexisting arthritis, such as an infected joint in a patient with RA or gout.
Is this flare up worse than usual? Suspicion for a superimposed process or infection should increase if the signs or symptoms are worse than prior gout, osteoarthritis, or autoimmune exacerbations.
Are there risk factors for infectious arthritis? Ask about sexual risk factors for gonococcal arthritis or reactive arthritis, IV drug use, tick bites, and travel history.

Are systemic symptoms of infection present? Although systemic symptoms may suggest infection, such symptoms are insensitive indicators of septic arthritis. Fever has a sensitivity of only 57% (95%, CI 52%-62%) for nongonococcal septic arthritis. Sweats and rigors have very low sensitivity for septic arthritis.Risk factors that significantly increase the likelihood of septic arthritis include age greater than 80 years, diabetes, recent joint surgery, and hip or knee prosthesis (especially if skin infection is also present).

Ask about other elements of history; psoriasis, uveitis, diarrhea, inflammatory bowel disease, or rash may suggest a spondyloarthritis such as psoriatic or reactive arthritis. Urethritis may point to gonococcal arthritis or reactive arthritis. Gout is more common in men with renal failure, heavy drinkers, and those who use diuretics.

Confirm by exam that an actual monoarthritis condition exists, involving the joint itself, and not a periarticular process such as bursitis, tendonitis, or cellulitis. Joint effusions signify intra-articular pathology and usually result in painful limitation of active and passive joint motion. Tendonitis may cause pain only on active motion that strains the involved tendon, and the tendon may be tender to palpation. Bursitis may cause swelling and erythema near the joint (eg, olecranon bursitis), but joint range of motion is usually preserved. Cellulitis usually extends beyond joint margins and is associated with minimal or no pain on joint motion, as opposed to the painful motion associated with inflammatory arthritis conditions. Very intense inflammatory arthritis, particularly gout and sometimes septic arthritis, can present with intense erythema of the skin that spreads well past the joint margins and can mimic cellulitis.
Signs of synovitis (soft tissue swelling, warmth over the joint, joint effusion) suggest an inflammatory arthritis and help focus the differential diagnosis.
See chapter on Knee injury (ligamentous) for more on diagnosis of meniscal and collateral ligament injuries.

Look for signs that suggest specific causes: (1) psoriatic skin plaques suggest psoriatic arthritis; (2) erythema nodosum suggests sarcoidosis or inflammatory bowel disease; (3) oral ulcers may suggest reactive arthritis, Behcet's disease, or systemic lupus; (4) skin ulcerations or infections may be a source of septic arthritis; and (5) subcutaneous nodules (tophi) and podagra (intense inflammatory arthritis of first MTP) are highly specific for gout. Additional clinical features supporting a diagnosis of gout are monoarticular involvement of a foot or ankle joint; prior episodes of similar acute arthritis; rapid onset of severe pain, swelling and erythema; male gender and associated cardiovascular diseases and hyperuricemia.

Septic arthritis most often arises from bacterial seeding of a joint and is much more likely to affect a large joint such as the knee (54%), hip (13%), or ankle (8%); low grade fever is often present.

Classic positioning of a septic hip in children is hip flexion, abduction and external rotation. Fever, refusal to bear weight, elevated white blood cell count, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and elevated C-reactive protein are helpful in differentiating septic arthritis from other conditions such as transient synovitis.
Joint infections caused by penetrating injuries most commonly occur in the finger joints.
Send the body fluid for cell count, culture, gram stain, and crystal studies.
If it is a prosthetic joint, ideally the surgeon should be notified before aspiration of body fluid if a swift response can be anticipated, and blood cultures should be drawn.

Serum testing is of limited value in evaluating monoarticular arthritis. Uric acid levels can be misleading in the workup of gout. Authors of a recent study, however, created a diagnostic rule for gout without requiring joint fluid analysis. They assigned points to 7 variables: male sex (2 points), previous arthritis attack (2 points), onset within 1 day (0.5 points), joint redness (1 point), involvement of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (2.5 points), the presence of hypertension or one or more other cardiovascular diseases (1.5 points), and serum uric acid level exceeding 5.88 mg/dL (0.35 mmol/L; 3.5 points). A score of 8 or greater was used as presumptive evidence for gout, a score between 4 and 8 requires joint fluid analysis, and a score of less than 4 suggests another etiology. The area under the receiver operator characteristic curve was 86%.

The delta neutrophil index which corresponds to the fraction of circulating immature granulocytes, assessed within 24 hours of hospitalization, was an independent predictor of septic over gouty arthritis in one case series, with an odds ratio of 14 using a cutoff of 1.9%. Only a small percentage of patients, however, had an elevated value (3.3 vs 0.6% for gouty arthritis).
Blood culture may assist in diagnosing septic arthritis, but joint aspiration is the gold standard.

Radiographs are helpful in patients with significant trauma or focal bone pain to rule out fracture or osseous tumor, and they may show relevant preexisting disease such as OA. However, radiographs are often not diagnostically helpful or show only nonspecific findings in acute or new monoarthritis. Radiographs sometimes help confirm the presence of joint effusions, and may show chondrocalcinosis in the involved joint (which suggests pseudogout). Radiographs are of greater value in assessing monoarticular pain in joints that are less reliably assessed by physical examination, such as the hip, sacroiliac joint, elbow, or ankle.The American College of Radiology (2022) recommend X-ray of the area of interest in patients with suspected osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, or soft-tissue infection (excluding spine and diabetic foot) and in cases of chronic extremity joint pain with suspected inflammatory arthritis.

Investigators found ultrasound (US) useful in detecting crystal deposition in 60 patients with suspected gout, with good agreement between US and synovial fluid analysis (k=0.87). Urate crystals were detected in 56.7% of first metatarsophalangeal, 63.3% of knee, and 51.7% of ankle joints. In this study, US detected significantly more patients with crystal deposition than dual-energy computed tomography (81.7% vs 56.7%, respectively).

In patients with suspected gout, especially in cases with no crystal identification and an atypical presentation, the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR, 2023) recommend US to seek features suggestive of monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition such as the double contour sign and tophi or duel-energy CT.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without and with intravenous contrast is recommended by the American College of Radiology following radiography in cases of suspected osteomyelitis or septic arthritis with cellulitis and a skin lesion, injury, wound, ulcer, or blister; history of prior surgery; site of previous non-arthroplasty hardware; and draining sinus, not associated with joint prosthesis. Authors of a review paper on pediatric hip septic arthritis noted that MRI is helpful in detecting concomitant infectious sites (e.g., osteomyelitis, pyomyositis and submuscular abscess).

Arthrocentesis for synovial fluid analysis is the most important test for evaluating acute or new onset monoarthritis in patients with joint effusions. Fluid should be sent for cell count and differential WBC count, cultures, Gram stain, and crystal analysis. Synovial fluid WBC counts of greater than 2000/mm3 suggest an inflammatory arthritis, with noninflammatory conditions such as uncomplicated OA and internal derangement of the joint producing WBC counts below this range. Hemarthrosis is present if the fluid obtained immediately on aspiration appears diffusely red, brownish, or pink, indicating that bleeding occurred before the aspiration. If the fluid was yellow when it first entered the syringe but then became bloody or blood tinged during the tap, this represents traumatic tap and not hemarthrosis. Synovial fluid is diagnostic for septic arthritis if a Gram stain or culture is positive. Gout or pseudogout is diagnosed if specific crystals are present when the fluid is assessed using a compensated polarized microscope. Arthrocentesis is mandatory if septic arthritis is suspected.

In a retrospective case series, of 172 joint aspirations for acute arthritis, 90 were positive for crystals (52.3%) and 24 (14%) were positive for bacteria. Features associated with bacteria in synovial fluid included sepsis, joint-restricted range of motion, elevated C-reactive protein and elevated total WBC count on synovial fluid.

In one case series of 673 children with monoarthritis, no child with an absolute neutrophil count <10 × 103 cells per mm and a sed rate <40 mm/hour had septic arthritis. The authors postulated that arthrocentesis could be omitted in such children.

Synovial fluid WBC counts: Traditional cutoff of greater than 50,000 WBC in the fluid has low sensitivity (62%) for septic arthritis. A wide range of synovial fluid WBC counts can be seen in patients with septic arthritis, and these cell counts overlap with cell counts seen in other inflammatory arthritic conditions. In one series, 6 of 61 patients with septic arthritis had synovial fluid WBC counts of less than 10,000 cells/mm3. As synovial fluid WBC count increases, there is a higher likelihood of infection (LR+ 2.9 for >25,000, LR+ 7.8 for >50,000, and LR+ 29 for >100,000/ul). Synovial fluid WBC counts less than 25,000/ul, sed rate less than 30 mm/hour, and peripheral WBC count less than 10,000 all reduce the likelihood of septic arthritis somewhat (LR− 0.17-0.32). Greater than % polymorphonuclear (PMN) cells is also helpful in diagnosing septic arthritis.

Synovial fluid cultures are an imperfect "gold standard" for diagnosing septic arthritis, with reported sensitivities of only 75% to 95% for nongonococcal septic arthritis.Synovial fluid should be quickly transferred to sterile tubes and plated as soon as possible. If enough synovial fluid is available, some authors recommend inoculating the fluid into blood culture bottles or blood microbial tube isolators to increase the likelihood of a positive culture result in septic arthritis. Gonococci are cultured from joints in less than 50% of cases of gonococcal arthritis. In practice, gonococcal cultures from joints will be routinely negative if the fluid is not immediately plated on prewarmed chocolate agar and immediately taken to the microbiology laboratory for incubation. Gonococcal cultures from appropriate mucosal sites of infection including the urethra, cervix, pharynx, or rectum, as well as blood cultures, are essential in attempting to confirm the diagnosis of disseminated gonococcal infection with arthritis. In Lyme arthritis, synovial fluid cultures are routinely negative despite evidence for spirochetes within the joint.

Synovial fluid cultures for fungal, tuberculosis (TB), and atypical mycobacterial arthritis require special culture techniques. Obtain such cultures in immunocompromised patients presenting with monoarthritis. Synovial fluid cultures for these organisms typically take a long period of time before becoming positive and have relatively low sensitivities (ie, 64%-79% for TB arthritis). The combination of synovial fluid culture, staining for acid-fast bacilli, and histological examination of synovium obtained by synovial biopsy is recommended if the suspicion for TB arthritis is high. Fungal arthritis, from various fungal organisms, often results in an indolent course of monoarthritis with delayed diagnosis resulting in part because synovial fluid cultures are often negative.

Gram stain and mycobacterial (AFB) stain in septic and TB arthritis: Sensitivity of Gram stain is only 29% to 50%.Ziehl–Neelsen stain (AFB stain) of synovial fluid was only 19% sensitive in one series.

When Gram stain and synovial fluid cultures are negative, diagnosis of septic monoarthritis may still require a clinical diagnosis using a combination of tests and observations. Factors that indicate septic arthritis in this setting include the presence of frank pus aspirated from a joint even when cultures and stains are negative, or the presence of positive cultures from other sources and observation of a clinical response to antibiotics.

Crystals
: Synovial fluid analysis for diagnosis of gout: The 2023 consensus guideline by EULAR recommends a search for crystals in synovial fluid or tophus aspirates for patients with suspected gout in cases when characteristic features of MSU crystal deposition on ultrasound or duel-energy CT are NOT identified, as MSU crystals allows a definite diagnosis of gout.

Sensitivity of routine laboratory analysis for monosodium urate (MSU) crystals that cause gout ranged from 63% to 78% when standard crystal preparations were used as test samples, showing significant dependence on observer ability. A multicenter case control study showed that in clinical practice, the identification of rules in gout, although the absence of crystal does not exclude this diagnosis.

Synovial fluid analysis for the diagnosis of pseudogout: Sensitivity of routine laboratory testing for calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals to diagnose pseudogout is significantly less than for MSU crystals, with sensitivities ranging from 12% to 83% based on a systematic review of the literature. False positives were also reported for CPPD specimens at a significant background rate in this review, so the odds for pseudogout were only increased by 2.9 after identification of CPPD crystals based on these studies.

Synovial fluid analysis for crystals other than MSU and CPPD: Hydroxyapatite and small calcium-containing crystals other than CPPD are only detectable by optical microscope if special stains such as alizarin red are used, or by use of electron microscopy. These tests are not available in standard laboratories. These forms of crystal-induced monoarthritis can be suspected based on recurrent clinical presentations, typically in a patient with renal failure, but they cannot be definitively diagnosed without access to special laboratories. The sensitivity and specificity of tests for these crystals is not known.

Fungal and mycobacterial monoarthritis often require synovial biopsy for histopathological staining and tissue culture for diagnosis. Synovial biopsy is also required to diagnose certain tumors including pigmented villonodular synovitis.

cell.label: Pain or swelling in a single joint. Perform history and physical examination
Significant trauma or focal bone pain?
Consider coagulopathy, trauma, pigmented villonodular synovitis, tumor, charcot joint, pseudogout.
Check prothrombin time/partial thromboplastin time, platelet count, bleeding time; obtain radiograph and, if negative, MRI.
Fat or other bone marrow elements?
Consider intra-articular fracture; obtain radiograph, MRI if negative.
Suspect monosodium urate (gout) or calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (pseudogout).
Positive synovial culture or Gram stain, or positive urethral, pharyngeal, rectal cultures when gonococcal arthritis is suspected?
If sterile inflammatory joint fluid, suspect spondyloarthritis, RA, SLE, sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, or mycobacterial or fungal infection in the appropriate clinical setting.
Osteoarthritis, internal derangement, soft tissue injury, viral infection.
